title: Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened.
author: Jonathan Mingle
content:
This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past
decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its
polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone
toward Lake Champlain.

“I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the
board’s chair.

Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten
for all that money. But that study was never done.

A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from
an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the
state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also
was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource
agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which
are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain.

## [Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica
Investigate Algae Blooms.](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/lake-
champlain-vermont-algae-bloom-pollution-callout)

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake
Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

[Get In Touch](https://propublica.jotform.com/263053595887977)

Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms,
roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic
blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s
tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental
advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders
embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality,
enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.

Now, halfway through a [20-year cleanup
effort](https://www.propublica.org/article/lake-champlain-algae-bloom-
cyanobacteria-water-pollution-vermont) mandated by the EPA, some lawmakers
worry they don’t have enough information to ensure that the state is pursuing
the most cost-effective cleanup strategies.

When lawmakers approved the clean water law, they took the major step of
establishing a fund to pay for the cleanup and a board to administer it. Since
2016, Vermont has disbursed $928 million — $755 million in state funding and
$173 million in local and federal dollars — on water quality projects and
programs. That’s nearly as much as what Vermont has spent on paving and
resurfacing state highways over the past decade.

As part of the law, the legislature also required the board’s leaders to
provide it with a full program audit by January 2021.

But the board received no responses to an initial request for proposals in
2020. Lawmakers extended the deadline to 2023. Yet again, no outside firms bid
on the audit.

Farnham said the board received informal feedback from some firms that the
audit’s scope was too broad and complex. He reported back to fellow board
members that he and Julie Moore, secretary of the Vermont Agency of Natural
Resources, had asked legislators what to do next but didn’t receive any clear
suggestions.

The board never issued a new request or revisited the matter (until Seven Days
and ProPublica recently asked about it), and Vermont’s legislature never
followed up to narrow the scope.

![A hand wearing a black glove holds a glass jar full of pea green
water.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-

content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_1592_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)St.
Albans in late August during a high-alert bloom day Volunteer photo courtesy
of Vermont Department of Health

Former state Rep. David Deen, who sponsored the clean water law and retired in
2018, said he was dismayed to learn that the audit never happened.

“Personally, I find it amazing that they haven’t done that audit and that
somebody in the legislature did not hold them to account to conduct that
audit,” he said.

Rep. Amy Sheldon, the longtime chair of the House Committee on Environment,
recalled hearing about the audit challenges but noted that it’s difficult for
the legislature to follow up because Vermont’s lawmakers don’t have staff. In
the other chamber, former state Sen. Chris Bray, who chaired the natural
resources committee until 2025, said he did not recall hearing about the
missing audit.

In an interview, Farnham acknowledged that an outside audit would be helpful.
But he said the board already has robust tools for assessing progress through
a yearly performance report compiled by the Vermont Department of
Environmental Conservation, which coordinates and tracks most of the state’s
clean water spending.

“We've got enough eyes coming at it from different angles that I think that
mutes the need for that comprehensive audit,” he said.

The annual reporting process has improved greatly since the audit was
mandated, and [the DEC’s website “provides a lot of
transparency,”](https://dec.vermont.gov/water-investment/cwi/state-vermont-
clean-water-projects/clean-water-portal) about how the state is spending clean
water money and the results, said Emily Bird, director of the department’s
Water Investment Division.

But some current and former state officials say that approach isn’t a
substitute for an audit to determine whether Vermont is getting adequate and
cost-effective returns on its huge water quality investments.

The last independent assessment of clean water spending was a 2019 report from
the state auditor. It found that a disproportionate amount of money was being
spent on wastewater treatment plants, which contributed by far the smallest
share of phosphorus pollution, instead of targeting bigger sources such as
agriculture.

That mismatch persists seven years later. Agriculture is the largest source of
phosphorus runoff, yet agricultural water quality programs receive less than a
third of the total clean water funding in the current budget.

“I’d like to think they’re getting something done,” said Doug Hoffer, state
auditor since 2013, referring to state agencies and legislators. “But the only
way to know that is to hire someone who is independent to study that. And it’s
really concerning that hasn’t been done. It really raises questions about
accountability on both sides.”

![An older man with gray hair wearing a suit and yellow tie. A row of red
shapes and people are out of focus behind him.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Doug-
Hoffer-045-crop_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=2560)Vermont Auditor Doug
Hoffer says the lack of an independent audit of Lake Champlain’s cleanup
efforts “raises questions about accountability.” Jeb Wallace-Brodeur/Seven
Days

An audit would do a few key things that the department’s performance reports
do not, Tee Thomas, a former water finance director for the state of Vermont
who now runs her own environmental consulting firm, noted via email. The
reports rely on models for how effective each type of project is at reducing
phosphorus. An audit would analyze water quality monitoring data from rivers
and lakes to check those estimates. It would also scrutinize how well Vermont
has managed projects and whether it’s gotten results, she said.

The Clean Water Fund gets, on average, $25 million to $30 million each year
from the state’s rooms and meals tax, a surcharge applied to some property
transfers and deposit money that consumers pay on cans and bottles. That money
is paired with between $6 million and $12 million from the state’s annual
capital bill, which finances infrastructure projects. The funds have gone to
programs and projects to restore wetlands, expand natural buffers around
fields, shore up rural roads against erosion, upgrade stormwater drains and
improve manure storage on dairy farms.

The state treasurer in 2017 [estimated that the
cost](https://www.vermonttreasurer.gov/sites/treasurer/files/committees-and-
reports/_FINAL_CleanWaterReport_2017.pdf) of Vermont’s 20-year initiative
would be $2.3 billion.

But finding that money could be difficult as state government spending
outpaces tax revenue and cooling housing and tourism markets squeeze clean
water funding sources.

Without the audit, the governor and legislators responsible for coming up with
the next billion dollars’ worth of projects may not have a clear understanding
of what Vermonters have gotten for the last billion, lawmakers said.

water-pollution-vermont)

Jane Kitchel, who as longtime chair of the state Senate’s Committee on
Appropriations was known for her encyclopedic knowledge of the Vermont budget,
noted that a billion dollars is a significant sum for the small state. Had she
not retired from the body two years ago, she said, reviving the audit “would
be one of the things I’d put on my to-do list.”

The next legislative session starts in January. State Sen. Anne Watson, who
chairs the Committee on Natural Resources and Energy and serves on the
Committee on Appropriations, told Seven Days and ProPublica that she would
likely discuss whether to revive the audit with her colleagues.

“If we value having a clean lake,” she said, “then we need to put our
resources toward places that are going to make a difference, and it's unclear
to me right now that what we’re doing is effective.”
